These show the kind of mistake. The weekly record keeps counts and does not yet list the props behind them, so we cannot point from a count to every prop. A truncated type is scored less precise, never wrong, so it is in the counts above only as less precise.

  • Right and present: the tool lists the prop and its type is the checker’s, or the same type spelled differently, such as by name where the checker expands it. A prop the tool leaves out counts against it.
  • Less precise: the tool’s type is looser or left unevaluated. It does not contradict the checker.
  • Wrong: the tool’s type describes something else. This is the number we gate on.
  • Not counted: the checker has no type either, as with an unresolved import.
type resolution

Unbound generics

A conditional or mapped type can stay opaque when its type parameter has no concrete value. Nested inference can leave part of a type unresolved.

component discovery

Anonymous wrappers

Some wrapper calls without a type argument and some styled-component forms are still missed by the default extractor.

A zero is not a clean bill. The comparison scores a lost Partial or Omit as less precise, not wrong; in Mantine that touches about 230 components’ classNames and styles. The experimental TypeScript 7.1 checker can recover some harder types on exported function components. It is opt-in and was off for these runs.

TypeScript’s checker does. It knows the type of every prop, so we ask it for each one and compare both tools with it by the same rules. RDT is not the reference. It prints the checker’s own type text, so it agrees on most props, and where it does not, it is sometimes the one that is wrong.

RDT’s list also holds entries that are not components: hooks, helpers and context providers, and one component repeated under every file that re-exports it. On Ant Design it lists 258 entries. With those taken out, 202 remain, and Caliper reports 186 of them (92.1%, November 2). A bar of “props found against RDT” would count the rest against Caliper, which is why it is not the headline here.

The comparison has known flaws in both directions, and the differences page lists each class with an example and whether the comparison scored it right.

Ant Design has no committed lockfile, so its dependencies are freshly resolved. The harness logs any other install that needs a fresh resolve. RDT and react-docgen run once each. The measurement page shows the timing boundaries.

result.output:
| `size` | `sm`, `md`, `lg`. One control scale (height, inline padding, text style) shared by every control. A test asserts that every component with `size` has the same height at each step; two named exceptions: SegmentedControl `sm`, which is the 24px nav toggle cell (`size.toggle.cell`) and meets the 24px target floor, not the 44px coarse-pointer target; and text inputs and Select (SPEC-008) use the `body` text style at every size, so their text never falls below `text.inputMin` (iOS Safari zooms a focused field under 16px). |
| `variant` | Visual emphasis within a component: `primary`, `secondary`, `ghost`. |
| `tone` | Semantic colour: `neutral`, `accent`, `danger`, `success`. Domain colour (an Orin tool `family`) maps to a tone. |
| `type` | Not a design prop. It stays the native attribute on buttons and inputs. |
| state | `disabled`, `pending`, `invalid`, `readOnly`, `required`, plus `pressed` or `selected` where the pattern needs one. Plain boolean names; wrappers translate React Aria's `isDisabled`. |
| values | `value`, `defaultValue`, `onValueChange(value)`. A single choice is a scalar and a multiple choice is an array, whatever the primitive returns. A control with no value yet takes `null` and renders its pending frame. Exceptions: Select's `null` means nothing is selected and the placeholder shows (its options are data, so its server HTML is never pending), and Menu's radio group `null` means no item is checked; RadioGroup uses `''` for none selected. |
| open state | `open`, `defaultOpen`, `onOpenChange(open)`. |
| position | `placement`, `offset`, `collisionPadding`, defaulting from tokens. |
| composition | `render` (element or `(props, state)`), `classes`, `ref` as a prop. No free `style` or `className`. |

### Markup

- The root carries `data-recipe`, `data-slot` and the design props as `data-size`, `data-variant`, `data-tone`.
- State is exposed only as our own attributes: `data-state` (`open | closed | on | off`, plus `mixed` on Checkbox), `data-orientation`, `data-disabled`, `data-pending`, `data-motion` (transition status: on overlays absent at rest, `starting` on enter and `ending` on exit; on SegmentedControl `ready` once the first paint has settled, so a known value never animates in), `data-current`, `data-highlighted` (Menu items and Select options, set by our wrapper). Design-time choices CSS needs are `data-placement`, `data-fill` and `data-modal` on overlays and `data-grouped` (`horizontal | vertical`) on a Button, Link or Toggle inside an attached group. Recipes style only these and ARIA attributes, never a library's own attributes, so swapping or upgrading a primitive never touches CSS.
- Parts are named by role: `Root`, `Trigger`, `Content`, `Item`, `Indicator`. We expose one anatomy of our own, not the primitive's (Base UI's `Positioner` and `Popup` are one `Content` to us).
- A control renders a pending frame of its own size while its state is unknown, and the real control the moment it has the state. It never renders a guess.

### Behaviour

Every default the primitive leaves open gets one decision, recorded in a table and tested: tab activation, whether a menu closes on selecting a check or radio item, hover delay, dismissal, focus return, Escape. The table is filled in per component when it is specified.

## Rules

Agreed 11 Oct:

1. Composition over configuration.
2. CSS before logic.
3. Mobile first; container queries over breakpoints. Media queries only for user preferences (motion, contrast, color scheme, hover, pointer, print, forced colors, scripting).
4. Semantic tokens at the design-system layer; components consume only semantic tokens.
5. `sva` and `cva` with semantic props, not `css()` and not inline style.
6. Never `!important`. Avoid inline style; it may carry a data-driven custom property (a swatch colour) and nothing else.

It didn't flow, so I restructured it. The page now reads as one argument: the checker first, then three evidence sections, then the Mantine causes. I screenshotted the full page at desktop width in light theme only. The `orin-dx` format, typecheck, lint and test checks all exit 0, and I did not run the site build or `verify`.

What was wrong and what changed:
- **Judge too late:** the checker's role came after five sections that relied on it. "Who decides what is right?" is now first, with a closing line that sets up the three questions.
- **Table interrupting the story:** the counts table sat between the coverage chart and the examples that explain RDT's 289. The examples now follow the wrong-count chart, and the counts table closes the evidence.
- **Examples added a consequence column:** each shows what a reader of the docs would see, such as "the wrong control for the prop" or "text that is not a type".
- **Falls-short cards replaced:** the generic cards are now Mantine's actual causes, from the record. Of its 40 unreported components, 26 are compound members such as `Combobox.Dropdown`, 6 are sub-components in files with others, 4 are helpers that aren't components and 4 are factory-built. Its 1,281 less-precise props come from aliases left unexpanded, with counts from the November 6 doc.
- **Redundant text trimmed:** I folded the Ant Design "258 entries, 202 remain" line into the coverage chart's note.

Where other pages still need work:
- **Measurement page:** it's still all October, 0.4.0, and it is the next page with this problem.
  - The "0.38 s cold" card and the cold-run chart are unsourced.
  - The "28× RDT median" and the request-time figures predate the lazy session and 0.10.0.
  - It has no narrative thread, no "how much better" detail (your earlier ask), and no per-library speed. I'd restructure it the same way: claim, how measured, evidence, limits.
- **Main Caliper page:**
  - The "Why Caliper" intro still opens with a generic claim.
  - The workflow evidence line is the October 24 number.
  - The 28× card is October 0.4.0.
  - The "Types in. Controls out." and "What those types look like" sections predate the checker story.
  - The roadmap and features still need the audit fixes: add "how it works", add a comparison, and show a real TOON sample.
- **Shared hero:** the kicker and the `art`/`meta` composition refactor are still waiting on your yes.
- **Dead code:** `ParityPlot` is unused and still in the repo.

The caveat that matters for trust is unchanged: the examples show kinds of mistake, not the actual 289, because the weekly record has counts and no per-prop rows. Fixing that is a Caliper-repo change.

Nothing in the pages repo is committed. Which page next: the measurement page, the main page, or the hero refactor?

- **Library bolding:** the bold first column makes the libraries stand out. A subtle shaded band on every other pair would help the eye further, but the `Table` component doesn't offer that and I didn't add it.

content.text:
Both fixes are in. The pairs in the counts table now scan at a glance, and the examples use the existing `TypeBoundaries` list instead of my local cards. I checked both at desktop width in light theme only. The `orin` and `orin-dx` gates (format, typecheck, lint, test) all exit 0, and I did not run the site build or `verify`.

**Pairs:**
- **Row colour:** each Caliper row is brass and its RDT row is muted. These are the same focus and reference colours the three charts use, so the table and the bars read as one system.
- **Group rule:** a heavier rule (2px against the hairline) closes each Caliper/RDT pair, and the last row still has none.
- **Library names:** the second row's name is muted too, so the bold names run down the column once per pair.
- **Table API:** I added two optional props to the existing `Table`: `groupSize` and `rowTones`. Both are plain data, and the recipe styles them through `data-*` attributes, per the rules. I added tests that cover marked groups, row tones and a table without either. I used props because `.astro` pages can't pass styled spans into a React component, and a new wrapper component was the thing you didn't want.

**Examples:** your critique was right on both counts: they were local cards in a 2×2 grid. They are now `TypeBoundaries` items stacked full width, with a highlighted code block per example and the declaration, RDT's output and the checker's in one block each. I made its `state` label optional, since "Works today" doesn't apply to a mistake. The "falls short" section uses `ItemGroups` (stack) in place of the other local cards. I deleted the five local style constants.

**Rough edges:**
- **Code blocks:** they show line numbers, because that's `TypeBoundaries`' default. For three-line snippets that is noisy, and I can turn them off for this use.
- **Rule weight:** the 2px rule is subtle on screen. A darker colour for the group rule would help, if the tokens have a suitable border colour. I haven't tried it.

Nothing is committed in the pages repo.

result: Counts table pairs now scan by role colour and a heavier group rule (via optional `groupSize` and `rowTones` on `Table`), and the examples use the existing `TypeBoundaries` list, with `orin` and `orin-dx` format, typecheck, lint and test exit 0, uncommitted in `~/projects/pages`.
Are we accounting for just components when counting the less precise column in the counts section?

No, not for RDT, and the page should say so. Here is what the record does and doesn't scope, and I'll fix the table's description.

- **Caliper's columns** (wrong, agrees, less precise): scored over the props of components Caliper reports. Caliper doesn't report helper functions as components, so they're out by construction. The record's `caliper` and `caliper_reported` figures are identical.
- **RDT's columns:** scored over every prop RDT lists in the checker's universe: any exported function whose parameter is a props type. RDT reports hooks, helpers and context providers as components. For React Spectrum, 291 of RDT's 1,319 entries were excluded as non-components, so some of its 138 wrong and 52 less-precise props may belong to things that aren't components. Mantine, Chakra, shadcn/ui and Ant Design have far fewer excluded entries (21, 73, 21, 43), but the same caveat applies.
- **Real components:** this column is the only one restricted to real components, via the cleaned reference list.

So the table compares Caliper-on-components against RDT-on-everything-it-lists. If anything that flatters Caliper's wrong count and inflates RDT's. I can't size the effect, because the record has no per-prop rows. The proper fix lives in the Caliper repo: score RDT on the cleaned component set too, and publish that as its own field. Until then the page should state the limit beside the table.

Every figure in the counts table matches the November 9 record exactly, so nothing is miscounted. The count of props across components is a misleading unit, though, and the shares tell a different story. The `orin-dx` format, typecheck, lint and test checks all exit 0. I looked at the table render before the final wording edits and didn't re-screenshot after.

**What the table was hiding**
- A "less precise" count of Chakra RDT 16,642 against Caliper 19 looked like a landslide. It is 3.2% against 0.004% of listed props, and Chakra's props are heavily repeated across components.
- On the share, Caliper is worse than RDT on three of five libraries: Mantine 6.4% against 2.9%, React Spectrum 5.0% against 1.9%, and Ant Design 5.7% against 5.2%. It is better only on shadcn/ui (5.0% against 10.9%) and Chakra.
- Every "wrong" and "less precise" cell now shows the count and its share of the props that tool lists, for example `9 (0.04%)` and `1,281 (6.4%)`. The description now states the unit: a prop on 700 components counts 700 times.
- The "Where Caliper falls short" description now names Spectrum as well as Mantine. We know Mantine's causes, but not Spectrum's, so the section says "here is what we know".
- The description paragraph is shorter than before.

**What I couldn't resolve: the agent's earlier caveat.** I read "wasn't so right" as the pasted note about the "completeness" label, which I already fixed. If the agent said something else about the counts that I haven't seen, paste it and I'll check it against the page. The record has no per-prop rows, so these things remain open:
- how much of RDT's wrong and less-precise counts comes from functions that aren't components;
- how many distinct causes sit behind the repeated props.

Both need the Caliper-side change I described, so the counts can be restricted to real components and deduplicated.

Nothing is committed in the pages repo.

result: Counts table figures all verified against the November 9 record, now shown as count plus share with the counting unit stated, and the falls-short section names Spectrum as well as Mantine, with `orin-dx` format, typecheck, lint and test exit 0, uncommitted in `~/projects/pages`.
Any similar improvements we can make to the measument page? The main caliper page?
Reading the measurement page as it stands, so the answer is specific rather than generic.

The shared harness costs about 0.32 s, so the measured gap inside extraction is larger than the end-to-end bars suggest. The 0.38 s result is not an isolated Rust timer.

This corpus is copied fixtures with no installed package tree. It is good for the three-tool comparison, but it cannot tell us how Caliper handles types from a real project’s dependencies.

Seven runs per library on an Apple Silicon laptop; Caliper’s shown time is its best wall time. The 28× headline is the median of five library ratios. Caliper’s clock includes process start and JSON output; RDT’s parse time excludes Node startup.

Chakra is the memory outlier: 1,461 MiB with dependencies loaded. The speedup alone would hide that cost.

For parity, each repo is pinned to a commit and installed with its own package manager. We remove tests, stories, demos and declaration files, then give both tools the same source files. Caliper uses full HTML attributes, includes unexported components and loads installed dependencies.

We match components by file and name. On shared components we count RDT’s non-React props that Caliper finds; on shared props we compare Storybook control kinds and type text. A separate TypeScript 7.1 checker run tests type structure because RDT is not ground truth. Explore the prop results.

The weekly parity run checks these rates against a committed baseline and flags growing loss patterns. When comparing a new build with a base build, the harness interleaves their runs and flags a slowdown over 10% on any library. The baseline’s old timing is a record, not the speed gate.
1

Save a file

The component source changes while Storybook stays open.

2

Check freshness

The session checks saved edits before answering a docgen request.

3

Resolve the story

The on-demand path asks for the component the story needs.

4

Return prop docs

Storybook gets argTypes, defaults and descriptions.

On-demand resolution shipped in the 0.10.0 addon. These source results predate it and are not package benchmarks.

The biggest win came from replacing a JavaScript directory sweep on every request with one native freshness check per story. Session startup also stopped sending every component’s props to JavaScript just to build an index.

These times cover the addon’s request path. They do not include browser rendering, Storybook’s UI work or a full page load. The before and after builds ran interleaved, best of three.
  • Version matters. The five-library parity numbers are Caliper 0.4.0 from October 23. Newer releases need the same run again.
  • The clocks differ. Cold Node startup is shared; installed-library Caliper time includes process start while RDT time does not; addon request time leaves out browser rendering.
  • Project shape matters. A large dependency graph can raise both latency and memory. The pinned repos expose that cost better than fixture files alone.
  • TypeScript 7.1 is separate. The checker is a measurement oracle. Caliper’s semantic extraction pass is an experimental CLI opt-in in source, not a Storybook feature yet.
  • Prop parity across five libraries
  • Back to Caliper

content.text:
The measurement page has the same problems the parity page had, and more. The main page is mostly fixed, with a few leftovers. Both pages should draw on the same November 9 weekly record the parity page now uses. I haven't changed either page yet.

**Measurement page**
- **Stale and wrong:**
  - Everything is October on Caliper 0.4.0, and the "0.38 s cold" figure and its chart are unsourced.
  - It says "the weekly parity run checks against a committed baseline". That's false: the baseline workflows were removed, and the previous run is the baseline.
  - "The checker is not a Storybook feature yet" is also out of date. The on-demand addon shipped in 0.10.0.
- **Current data is available.** The November 9 record has wall time and peak memory for all five libraries:

  | Library | Caliper | RDT | Speed ratio | Caliper memory | RDT memory |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Mantine | 286 ms | 4.7 s | 16× | 219 MiB | 539 MiB |
  | Chakra | 903 ms | 59 s | 66× | 451 MiB | 2,084 MiB |
  | shadcn/ui | 629 ms | 10.2 s | 16× | 353 MiB | 1,400 MiB |
  | Ant Design | 156 ms | 6.1 s | 39× | 179 MiB | 1,038 MiB |
  | React Spectrum | 274 ms | 6.0 s | 22× | 233 MiB | 816 MiB |

  The median is about 22×. This is on a CI machine, and the October 28× was on a laptop, so the page must not mix them.
- **Honest caveats to carry:** Caliper's time is the median of five runs and the others are single runs. The Storybook first answer on the large gate project is 402 to 562 ms against a 150 ms target, a failed gate in ADR 0026. A "limits before claims" page should say that.
- **Proposed shape, same as the parity page:**
  1. Claim: faster, lighter, and fast in Storybook.
  2. How it was measured.
  3. Per-library time as `ComparisonBars` (scaled per library, since the ratio is the story), then memory.
  4. Storybook request path: the lazy first story, 55–121 ms against 357–425 ms, from the changelog.
  5. Counts table with paired rows.
  6. Limits.

**Main Caliper page**
- **Remaining from the audit:**
  - The 28× card is the October laptop figure, so it should become the current 22× median, with the CI caveat.
  - The "Go deeper" "4 ms" card is October.
  - The "Why Caliper" intro should lead with a finding (2 wrong against 289, 89% to 98% of real components) instead of a generic claim.
  - The page still lacks a "how it works" section, a comparison with react-docgen and RDT, and a real TOON sample for agents.
  - The roadmap should name the checker-as-default step honestly, including the failed first-answer gate.
- **Hero:** the kicker and the `art`/`meta` slot refactor are still waiting on your yes.

**Shared fix:** put the November 9 values in one typed data module with their date and source, and have all three pages read from it. Today they're hard-coded in the parity page and the page data, so the figures can drift.

I'd do it in this order: the shared data module, then the measurement page, then the main page's figures and intro, then "how it works" and the comparison table. Shall I start with the data module and the measurement page?

We want to make sure we call our not just speed but memory also, ther improvement ratios. Don't overlwem uses by cramming it all at once and consider the flow and narrative

Bars show the slower end of each range: lazy 55 to 121 ms, eager 357 to 425 ms. The answers are identical.', } as const const protocol = [ { label: 'pin', title: 'Pin real projects', text: 'Five public repos at fixed commits, installed with their own package managers. content.text:
The measurement page is rebuilt, and the main page's figures now come from the same dated record as the parity page. The `orin-dx` format, typecheck, lint and test checks all exit 0. I screenshotted the new measurement page in full and the main page's "How it stacks up" section at desktop width in light theme only. I did not re-screenshot after the last deep-dive card tweak, and did not run the site build or `verify`.

**The headline, speed and memory together:** across the five libraries, Caliper is 16× to 66× faster than RDT (median 22×) and uses 2.5× to 5.8× less memory (median 4×). The memory side is called out as prominently as the speed side. For Chakra, RDT takes 59 s and 2,084 MiB; Caliper takes 903 ms and 451 MiB. That is the November 9 weekly record on a CI runner.

**Measurement page flow:** one idea per section, each description bridging to the next.
- **Opening:** the claim, with both ratios.
- **"How we measured":** three short steps.
- **"1 · speed" and "2 · memory":** one chart each, with the ratio on every pair. The speed chart scales each pair on its own, because the ratio is the story.
- **"3 · Storybook":** two charts from the 0.10.0 changelog on Chakra. The lazy session answers its first story in 55 to 121 ms against 357 to 425 ms eager, and uses 419 MB against 658 MB.
- **"The numbers behind the bars":** the paired-row table.
- **"Where it falls short":** four bullets. The large-project first answer is 402 to 562 ms against a 150 ms target, a failed gate in ADR 0026. CI timing is noisy. Caliper's time is a median of five runs and RDT's is one run. Session memory was measured on macOS arm64 only.

I removed the unsourced "0.38 s" chart, the October laptop table, the false "committed baseline" claim and the filler four-step diagram.

**One shared record:** the new `data/caliperRecord.ts` holds the November 9 figures with their date. The parity page, measurement page, main page figures, and the family metrics all read from it. The deep-dive card now shows the per-library range (16–66× and 2.5–5.8×), so it adds something beyond the 22× card above it. The stale roadmap line is replaced with the real open work.

**Still open:**
- **Main page:** the "how it works" section, the comparison with react-docgen and RDT, a real TOON sample, and the "Why" intro leading with a finding.
- **Hero:** the kicker and the `art`/`meta` slot refactor are still waiting on your yes.
- **Dead code:** `ParityPlot` is unused.
- **Caliper-side change for trust:** score RDT on real components and list the props behind each count. Not planned yet.
- **Not committed:** nothing in the pages repo is committed.

content.text:
The tool pages and Caliper's two evidence pages now have a chapter list: numbered entries in the left rail with a "Back to top" link, and the content on the reading column beside it. The `orin-dx` format, typecheck, lint and test checks all exit 0. `orin-dx:build` built all 16 pages and `orin-dx:verify` reported "16 pages checked, ok" (dead links, anchors, alt text).

I looked at the parity page at desktop and phone width, and the main Caliper page and Wisp at desktop width, in light theme only. I did not look at the other seven tool pages, the measurement page's final render or dark theme. The checks cover the other seven only through the build.

The mechanism: the evidence layout and the shared `[tool].astro` template now use the system's `DocumentPage`, the same one Principles uses. All nine tool pages (the template builds the chapter list from the same conditions that decide which sections exist) and Caliper's two sub-pages get it. The trail sits above the document as the breadcrumbs design doc requires. The hero is the document's lead, so `ToolHero` and `ToolPageHero` gained a `headingId`.

Details and caveats:
- **Sections:** they are now `frame` width with a small spacing wrapper, as Principles does it, because `PageSection` doesn't space children in that mode. Section labels are plain words (such as "the job" and "wrong types"), because the rail numbers them.
- **Phone width:** on the parity page the rail isn't visible in the viewport. I'd expect it to move into the menu as the system's chapter design does, but I did not open the menu to confirm.
- **Side effect on tool pages:** the right-hand source notes now sit after each section's content instead of beside it. The Caliper main page shows the same arrangement. If you'd like them back in the rail, that needs a layout decision for document pages.
- **The 'text' mistake:** I first tried `width="text"` and the sections spilled across the rail, which is why the pages use `frame`.

A backup of the original template is in the job's tmp folder. Nothing is committed. The pages repo has 19 changed or new files: the hero and table components, the lattice level, the shared data, the three Caliper pages, the template and two docs and stories.

Open items:
- the kicker/slot refactor, still waiting on your yes;
- the unused `ParityPlot`;
- the Caliper-side change to score RDT on real components and list the props behind counts.

Exit code 1
67
# Evidence and documentation language

Status: proposal for review. This records the visual and component direction for Orin DX tool pages; it does not approve token changes.

## The jobs

A product page makes one promise, shows one concrete result, gives a measured reason to believe it, then links to the details. A documentation page lets an engineer inspect the input, output, method, version and limits without decoding decorative color.

The current roles cover page surfaces, family identity, type, status and one measurement accent. They do not yet say how to color multiple data series or distinguish a measured result from an estimate. Orin's `surface.sunken` also resolves to the same color as `surface`, so it cannot by itself create a distinct source pane.

Code has its own seven semantic roles in the Orin Panda theme: keyword, literal, type, callable, scalar, parameter and comment. They reference brass, verdigris, lilac, sky, rose, lime and muted ink respectively. They describe syntax, not tool family or pass/fail status. Light code uses deeper inks that reach at least 6.8:1 on the pale code pane; dark code uses the brighter brand partners on Case. Plain text remains body ink. Punctuation stays muted, and the grammar's token classes decide where each role appears. The Button source specimen uses the same highlighter as the setup examples.

Across tool pages, the problem and answer stack on one reading line. Short, reviewed feature groups can use numbered editorial rows; longer lists keep cards so they remain scannable. Raw agent-visible output remains plain text so the specimen shows the bytes an agent receives; source code and commands use syntax colors. Long raw-output lines wrap visually inside their frame without changing the sample text.

## Color by meaning

| Job | Proposed roles | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One comparison | `data.focus`, `data.reference`, `data.track`, `data.rule` | The subject gets one emphasis; every value is labeled. The track is scaffolding, never a data series. |
| Multiple categories | `data.series.1` to `.5` | A curated order, stable within one figure and legend. Use a gap or keyline where neighboring colors touch. Do not borrow family colors as family labels. |
| Magnitude | `data.sequential.1` to `.5` | One ordered lightness ramp. More color means more of the named quantity in both themes. |
| Change around zero | `data.diverging.low`, `.mid`, `.high` | Two directions from a neutral midpoint. State the direction in text and show a zero rule. |
| Outcome | Existing `status.pass`, `.warn`, `.fail` | Reserve for actual outcomes, with a word and icon. A fast result is not a “pass” by color alone. |
| Metrics | Existing `text.measure` | Value first, then what it measures, then method/version/date in muted type. No colored number without its unit and scope. |
| Evidence surfaces | `surface.evidence`, `surface.source`, `surface.output` | Name the jobs before adding new colors. Start as aliases to existing `surface`, `surface.sunken` and `bg.canvas`; add a primitive only if the paired panes still merge in both themes. |

The first single-comparison mapping can alias `data.focus` to `text.measure`, `data.reference` to `text.muted`, `data.track` to `surface.raised`, and `data.rule` to `border.control`. The five-category scale needs a curated light/dark sequence from the existing hue ramps, then chart-specific values if family associations or adjacent-color checks make those unsuitable. The semantic aliases keep chart choices out of page code.

In the current Caliper figures, brass means “read this series first.” It marks Caliper in the three-tool race and “after” in the request comparison; it does not mean success or identify the build family. The tool name and before/after labels make those subjects explicit. Rose identifies the build family in product navigation and artwork, not a bar's outcome. Green is reserved for a labeled status such as pass; a shorter time or higher parity is described in words, not declared good by hue. Parity's props found and same-control values are peer measures, so they share one data color and keep their direct labels. Do not assign a new color just to make a second bar different.

An initial five-series sequence, for figures that truly need five categories:

| Series | Orin light | Orin dark | Source primitive |
| ------ | ---------- | --------- | ---------------- |
| 1      | `#2c779e`  | `#6bc4eb` | sky 700 / 400    |
| 2      | `#b63c62`  | `#ed9cb1` | rose 700 / 400   |
| 3      | `#597c19`  | `#9bca44` | lime 700 / 400   |
| 4      | `#744ed7`  | `#bea9f3` | lilac 700 / 400  |
| 5      | `#22695f`  | `#99e1d9` | verdigris        |

Each candidate exceeds 4:1 against the current Orin `surface` in light mode and 8:1 in dark mode. Those figures establish visibility against the panel, not separation between touching series. The visual review should test the ordered sequence with realistic bars, lines and legends, including color vision simulation. Use as many series as the data needs; five is a ceiling for this first pass, not a target.

Test meaningful bars, points, rules and neighboring regions against their adjacent colors at 3:1. Text stays at 4.5:1. Labels, shape, ordering and direct values carry the meaning when color is unavailable. Check both Orin themes and both techworx modes before promoting shared roles. [Carbon's palette guidance](https://www.carbondesignsystem.com/building-blocks/data-visualization/color-palettes) distinguishes categorical, sequential, diverging and alert palettes; [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag/) supplies the contrast and non-color requirements.

## Component grammar

| Pattern | Content | Recipe contract |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `EvidenceFigure` | Title, direct labels, unit, method, version/date, source link and caveat | `sva` slots for frame, plot, caption and method; `cva` for a small set of `kind` variants such as comparison, category and change. |
| `Metric` | Value, label, scope and provenance | `sva` slots keep the lower text aligned across a set. A `state` variant says measured, preliminary estimate or source experiment in words; it does not change only color. |
| `SourceOutput` | Real input beside actual generated output | `sva` slots for source, output and caption. Equal treatment for peer fields. A `selected` variant exists only for an actual interactive selection. |
| `DocumentLink` | A title, a useful preview and an affordance | `sva` slots for body and footer; a `cva` variant may express hover/selected behavior. No strand edge. |
| `EvidenceNote` | A nearby source, caveat or definition | Use the existing icon-led margin-note recipe and label the note's job. |
| `ReleaseNotice` | What ships now, what is in source and what is experimental | Text and version do the work; tone variants are for genuine warning or availability states. |

Use `sva` when parts of one component need coordinated styling and `cva` for a single element with meaningful variants. Put reusable recipes beside their components, and promote them to foundations only when two pages or brands need the same contract. Page-level `css()` remains appropriate for a one-off layout arrangement; it should not encode chart color or repeat the anatomy of a component.

## Decoration and rhythm

- Family color and tint identify a tool or family. They do not stand in for data status or a selected row.
- The strand edge belongs to a primary product answer or a real brand illustration. Charts, document links, source panes and ordinary cards rely on typography and alignment.
- A document moves from summary to figure to method to reference. One focal point per screen; the dense material comes later.
- Long tool documents should use the existing chapter rail from `DocumentPage`, with source notes beside the claims they support.

## First application

Caliper's cold-run and addon-request charts now use slot recipes with focus/reference fill variants. The parity chart directly labels its two measures and uses one brass data fill; its Button fixture uses a source/output slot recipe with peer prop rows. The parity and measurement pages share note/explanation spacing through a small recipe. Callisto, Michi, Monokl and Wisp use the same source-note and code treatments, with numbered feature rows only where the copy is short enough to scan. Longer pages keep their card groups. The five-series sequence remains a proposal to test in both themes before updating the brand library source and generated semantic tokens together.

# Design system API reference

Reference for the five design-system packages in this workspace: the exports map of each, then for each exported component its props, slots, emitted attributes and accessibility behaviour. Everything is derived from `package.json`, the TypeScript source, the slot recipes and the tests beside them.

The reference is structured per package and per component so a section can be regenerated when its source changes. To regenerate a component section, read its `.tsx` file for the props type, its `*Recipe.ts` (or the package's `recipes.ts`) for slots, variants and default variants, and its tests for what is asserted. Generated output (`styled-system`, `dist/panda`) is gitignored; read recipe definitions, not generated files.

## Contents

- `@pages/foundations`: Panda presets, tokens, the layout frame and slot helpers
- `@pages/components`: shared components and helpers
- `@pages/twx`: techworx components
- `@pages/orin`: Orin DX components
- `@pages/cv-kit`: the CV page shell

table = """#### Table

- Import: `import { Table } from '@pages/orin/Table'` (also exports type `TableProps`)
- Source: `packages/orin/src/table/table.tsx`; recipe: `tableRecipe` in `packages/orin/src/table/tableRecipe.ts`.
- Tests: `packages/orin/src/table/table.test.tsx`.
- What it renders: a keyboard-focusable scroll region named by the caption, holding a `<table>` with a mono column-label row. The first cell of each row is its row header.
- Usage: in use. Consumers in apps: orin-dx: tool pages, the Caliper evidence pages.

**Props**

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `caption` | `string` | required | Names the scroll region and the table. |
| `hideCaption` | `boolean` | `false` | Keeps the caption for assistive technology and does not draw it, when a heading above names the table. |
| `columns` | `readonly string[]` | required | The column labels. Keep each to one short word where you can: a heading that repeats a tool's name across columns reads badly. Put the tool in a column instead (one row per tool). |
| `rows` | `readonly (readonly ReactNode[])[]` | required | One array of cells per row. |
| `groupSize` | `number` | none | Rows that belong together, such as a Caliper row and its RDT row: a heavier rule closes each group. |
| `rowTones` | `readonly ('focus' \\| 'reference' \\| undefined)[]` | none | The role of each row by index, in the colours the charts use: `focus` is the subject in `text.measure`, `reference` is what it is held against in `text.muted`. |
| `classes` | `{ root?, table?, caption?, head?, cell? }` (strings) | none | Appended per slot by `mergeSlots`. |
| `...rest` | `ComponentPropsWithRef<'div'>` minus `children`, `className` | none | Spread onto the root `<div>`. |

**Attributes emitted**: `data-recipe="table"` on the root, `data-slot` on each part, `data-group-end` on every cell of the last row of a group, `data-tone` on every cell of a toned row.

**Accessibility**:

- The root is `role="region"` with `aria-label` equal to the caption and `tabIndex={0}`, so a table wider than its column scrolls by keyboard.
- Colour is never the only carrier: a toned row also names its tool in a cell, and the values are always written out.

"""
replace_once("#### PageSection\n", table + "#### PageSection\n")
open(path, 'w', encoding='utf-8').write(text)
print('api reference updated')
EOF

# Measurement

Two things, both small: a weekly record of how Caliper compares with react-docgen-typescript (RDT) and react-docgen on five public repos, and `just bench` for a change that touches the resolver. Nothing here blocks a pull request.

## Weekly record

`.github/workflows/weekly.yml` runs on Mondays and by hand. `scripts/corpora.py` fetches each repo at a pinned commit and installs its dependencies with its own package manager and lockfile (lifecycle scripts off, caches under `.corpora/`, gitignored), then removes tests, stories, demos and the `dist/` and `build/` directories from the source directory so every tool reads the same files. `scripts/weekly.py` runs the tools.

Declaration files are kept. Until 2026-11 the fetch also deleted every `.d.ts`, which removed a corpus's own type packages: React Spectrum declares `@react-types/shared` in `packages/@react-types/shared/src/*.d.ts` and its components import from it. With those files gone, 20 props that reach a component through `Pick` of a name declared there were lost; on unmodified main with the files restored, Caliper reports 20 of 20. Generated declarations sit in `dist/` and `build/`, which are still removed. A fetched corpus records a prune version in its marker (`PRUNE_VERSION` in `scripts/corpora.py`), so one pruned under the older rule is fetched again on the next `setup`; `--sparse` never pruned and already kept declaration files. This comparison between tools is information, never a gate, and the rules were validated on antd and shadcn; the weekly run produces all five corpora.

### The headline

What matters is whether the types Storybook and agents are shown are right, not whether Caliper matches RDT. The headline (`scripts/headline.py`, read from `oracle.tools.caliper_reported`, which `apps/oracle/src/tool-score.ts` `scoreReported` computes) takes every own prop the checker finds on a component Caliper reports, so a function the checker takes for a component and Caliper rightly ignores does not count against it, and sorts each prop into one kind:

- **Correct**: the same type as the checker, or the same type spelled differently.
- **Less precise**: vaguer than the checker's (a name left unexpanded, `string` for a union of literals), not contradicting it.
- **Wrong**: describes something else. This is the gate.
- **No checker type**: the checker has none either (an unresolved import, `any`).
- **Missing**: Caliper reports the component but not the prop.
- **Named only**: Caliper lists the prop by name as a member of a collapsed inheritance layer, so it is surfaced but a reader sees no type for it. It is counted apart, as neither correct nor wrong, because correct values reached through a layer are a win and a bare name is not.

The record keeps the counts per corpus as `headline`, next to the unchanged `oracle` and `recall` fields. The shares in the summary are of every prop of the components Caliper reports. The gate uses the wrong share of the props whose type can be judged (correct, less precise and wrong), so a corpus with many layer-only props does not dilute it.

The weekly record collapses nothing (`--collapse-inherited-props none`), so named only is 0 there; its run of 2026-11-06 reads antd 94.0% correct, 6.0% less precise, 0 wrong, and shadcn 93.8% correct, 5.3% less precise, 8 wrong (0.058% of the shared props), 0.4% missing (`headline` in `weekly.json`, `main` at `c5fbb33e`). Mantine, Chakra and Spectrum read in that run: 90.9%, 100.0% and 83.7% agree, with 0, 1 and 22 wrong. Of Spectrum's 22, the comparator's index-signature artifact accounts for all (`docs/rdt-differences.md`), so that gate firing is false until the comparator is corrected.

### An independent reference

The oracle above scores a tool against the TypeScript checker alone. That cannot judge a mode that uses the checker, which would agree with itself, and it cannot say which side is right when they differ. `scripts/reference_sample.py` (`apps/oracle/src/reference.ts`) judges a sample of props by two methods that fail differently:

- **A, the checker's type.** The same normalized type the oracle compares (`oracle-checker.ts`).
- **B, the declared type.** What the prop's declaration writes, read from source text with TypeScript's parser (`reference-declared.ts`), never from the checker's type printer. The checker is asked only where the declaration is. B abstains where the declaration leaves the type to be computed (an indexed access, `keyof`, a conditional type), writes no type (an unannotated member, a method with no return type, or a value such as `count: 1` in an object literal that the checker infers the type of), has no declaration (a mapped type's synthesized member), or has several that differ.
